notes:
1. Meaning of Federalism

Federalism is a system in which powers are constitutionally divided between:

  • Union Government.
  • State Governments.
  • Both levels derive their authority from the Constitution.
  • Each operates within its constitutionally assigned sphere.
  • Neither level is subordinate to the other in matters constitutionally assigned to it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Federalism → Constitutional Division of Powers between Union and States

2. Meaning of Federation

A Federation consists of:

  • National Government.
  • Regional or State Governments.

Both levels:

  • Govern the same territory.
  • Exercise authority directly over the people.
  • Derive powers from the Constitution.

3. Essential Federal Features

A federal system generally possesses:

  • Written Constitution.
  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Division of powers.
  • Independent Judiciary.
  • Bicameral Legislature.
  • Rigid Constitution.
  • Dual Government.

4. Purpose of Federalism

Federalism seeks to balance:

  • National unity.
  • Regional autonomy.

It enables governance at:

  • National level.
  • State level.

5. Why India Adopted Federalism

India required federal arrangements because of its:

  • Vast territory.
  • Large population.
  • Linguistic diversity.
  • Cultural diversity.
  • Religious diversity.
  • Regional differences.
  • Administrative needs.

6. Federalism and National Integration

Indian Federalism allows States to preserve:

  • Language.
  • Culture.
  • Regional identity.

while maintaining:

  • National unity.
  • National integration.
  • Constitutional governance.

7. Government of India Act, 1919

The 1919 Act introduced:

  • Dyarchy in Provinces.
  • India nevertheless remained predominantly centralised.
  • It represented an early stage in the development of federal principles.

8. Government of India Act, 1935

The Government of India Act, 1935 provided important federal foundations through:

  • Provincial Autonomy.
  • Three Legislative Lists.
  • Federal Court.
  • Distribution of legislative powers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Government of India Act, 1935 → Major Constitutional Source of Indian Federalism

9. Constituent Assembly Approach

The Constituent Assembly sought to combine:

  • Strong national unity.
  • Effective State Governments.
  • Administrative flexibility.
  • Constitutional balance.

The result was:

  • Federal structure.
  • Strong Union features.

10. Article 1

Article 1 declares:

  • “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.”

The Constitution does not use the word:

  • “Federal”
  • to describe India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1 → India = Union of States

11. Why the Expression “Union of States” Was Used

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explained that:

  • Indian Union is not the result of an agreement among sovereign States.
  • States possess no right to secede.
  • Union is permanent.
  • State boundaries may be altered by Parliament.

12. Indestructible Union

The source describes India as:

  • An indestructible Union of destructible States.

This reflects:

  • Permanence of Union.
  • Parliament's power to reorganise States.

13. Nature of Indian Federalism

India possesses both:

  • Federal features.
  • Unitary features.

Therefore, it is often described as:

  • Quasi-Federal.
  • Federal with a Strong Centre.
  • Cooperative Federal.

14. Meaning of Quasi-Federal

Quasi-Federal means:

  • Neither completely federal.
  • Nor completely unitary.

India combines:

  • Constitutional division of powers.
  • State Governments.

with:

  • Extensive Union authority.

15. K.C. Wheare

K.C. Wheare described the Indian Constitution as:

  • Quasi-Federal.

His description emphasised:

  • Predominance of Union Government within the federal framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

K.C. Wheare → Quasi-Federal

16. Granville Austin

Granville Austin described Indian Federalism in terms of:

  • Cooperative Federalism.

The emphasis is on:

  • Cooperation.
  • Consultation.
  • Shared governance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Granville Austin → Cooperative Federalism

17. Dual Polity

India has two principal constitutional levels:

  • Union Government.
  • State Governments.

Both:

  • Derive power directly from Constitution.
  • Function within constitutional spheres.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dual Polity → Federal Feature

18. Written Constitution

India has:

  • A written Constitution.

A written Constitution clearly defines:

  • Union powers.
  • State powers.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Constitutional institutions.

19. Supremacy of the Constitution

The Constitution is:

  • Supreme Law of the Land.

Neither:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures
  • may act contrary to it.

20. Judicial Review

An unconstitutional law may be declared invalid by:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.

Judicial Review therefore protects:

  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Federal balance.

21. Independent Judiciary

The Judiciary:

  • Interprets Constitution.
  • Protects Fundamental Rights.
  • Resolves Union–State disputes.
  • Maintains constitutional supremacy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Independent Judiciary → Essential Federal Feature

22. Bicameral Parliament

The Union Legislature consists of:

  • Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha.

Rajya Sabha represents:

  • States within Parliament.

23. Rajya Sabha as Federal Chamber

  • Rajya Sabha provides State representation at Union level.

However:

  • States do not receive equal representation.
  • Representation is broadly population-based.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rajya Sabha → Represents States

But → Equal Representation of States? No

24. Rigidity of Federal Provisions

Certain constitutional amendments affecting federal provisions require:

  • Special Majority in Parliament.
  • Ratification by at least one-half of State Legislatures.

25. Flexible Features

Other constitutional changes may be made through:

  • Simple Majority.

India's Constitution is therefore:

  • Partly rigid.
  • Partly flexible.

26. Division of Legislative Powers

The Seventh Schedule divides legislative subjects into:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seventh Schedule → Union + State + Concurrent Lists

27. Single Constitution

India generally operates under:

  • One Constitution

for both:

  • Union.
  • States.
  • The source notes the historical special position of the former State of Jammu and Kashmir before the constitutional developments of 2019.

28. Single Citizenship

India provides:

  • Single Citizenship.

There is:

  • No separate State citizenship.

Every citizen is:

  • Citizen of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Single Citizenship → Unitary Feature

29. Strong Union

The Union Government possesses:

  • Wider legislative field.
  • Greater financial resources.
  • Wider administrative authority.
  • This gives Indian Federalism a strong central tendency.

30. Residuary Powers

Residuary legislative powers belong to:

  • Parliament.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 248.
  • Entry 97 of Union List.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 248 + Union List Entry 97 → Residuary Powers → Parliament

31. Parliament and State Boundaries

Under Article 3, Parliament may:

  • Form new States.
  • Alter boundaries.
  • Increase or reduce territory.
  • Change State names.

32. State Consent under Article 3

  • State Legislature's views are sought under constitutional procedure.
  • State consent is not mandatory.
  • This is treated as a strong Union or unitary feature.

33. Governors

Governor is appointed by:

  • President of India.

This creates an institutional link between:

  • Union.
  • States.

34. Integrated Judiciary

India has one integrated judicial system:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.
  • Subordinate Courts.
  • There are no completely separate federal and State court systems of the classical federal type.

35. All India Services

Important examples include:

  • IAS.
  • IPS.
  • Indian Forest Service.

These officers serve within both:

  • Union framework.
  • State administration.

36. Emergency Provisions

During:

  • National Emergency.
  • President's Rule.
  • Financial Emergency
  • Union authority expands substantially.
  • This can make the federal system operate in a more unitary manner.

37. Integrated Election Machinery

Election Commission of India conducts elections to:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures.
  • This creates a common national electoral mechanism.

38. Integrated Constitutional Institutions

Common constitutional institutions include:

  • Election Commission.
  • Comptroller and Auditor General.
  • Union Public Service Commission.
  • Finance Commission.
  • These contribute to national constitutional integration.

39. Federal–Unitary Balance

Federal features include:

  • Dual polity.
  • Written Constitution.
  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Division of powers.
  • Independent Judiciary.
  • Bicameral Parliament.
  • Rigid federal provisions.

Unitary features include:

  • Strong Union.
  • Single Constitution.
  • Single Citizenship.
  • Residuary power with Parliament.
  • Parliament's power over State boundaries.
  • Governors appointed by President.
  • Integrated Judiciary.
  • All India Services.
  • Emergency provisions.

40. Article 245

Article 245 provides:

  • Parliament may legislate for whole or any part of India.
  • State Legislature may legislate for whole or any part of its State.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 245 → Territorial Extent of Legislative Powers

41. Article 246

Article 246 distributes legislative competence through:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 246 → Distribution of Legislative Powers

45. State List

The State List contains subjects of:

  • Local importance.
  • Regional importance.
  • State Legislatures generally possess legislative power over these matters.

48. Concurrent List

Concurrent List contains subjects on which both:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures

49. Concurrent List — Number of Subjects

According to the source:

  • Originally → 47 subjects.
  • Presently → 52 subjects.

50. Important Concurrent List Subjects

Examples include:

  • Civil Procedure.
  • Marriage and Divorce.
  • Adoption.
  • Education.
  • Forests.

51. Article 254

Article 254 deals with inconsistency between:

  • Parliamentary law.
  • State law
  • on Concurrent List subjects.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 254 → Repugnancy on Concurrent List

52. General Rule of Repugnancy

Where a Parliamentary law and State law conflict on a Concurrent List subject:

  • Parliamentary law prevails.
  • State law becomes inoperative to the extent of inconsistency.

53. Presidential Assent Exception

If a State law on a Concurrent List matter:

  • Receives President's assent,

it may prevail:

  • Within that State.

However:

  • Parliament may later override it by subsequent legislation.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Concurrent Conflict → Union Law Prevails

State Law + Presidential Assent → May Prevail in That State

Parliament → Can Later Override

54. Meaning of Residuary Subjects

Residuary subjects are matters not enumerated in:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

55. Examples of Emerging Residuary Areas

The source gives modern examples such as:

  • Cyber laws.
  • Digital currencies.
  • Artificial Intelligence regulation.
  • Space technology
  • where the matter is not otherwise covered by an existing entry.

56. Why Residuary Powers Belong to Parliament

The source explains that this arrangement supports:

  • National unity.
  • Uniform regulation of emerging subjects.
  • Legislative flexibility for new technologies.

57. Article 249

Parliament may legislate on State List if:

  • Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.
  • Resolution declares legislation necessary in national interest.

Majority required:

  • Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 249 → Rajya Sabha + State List + National Interest + 2/3 Present & Voting

58. Article 250

During:

  • National Emergency,

Parliament may legislate on:

  • State List subjects.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 250 → State List during National Emergency

59. Article 251

Article 251 provides that Parliamentary laws under:

  • Article 249.
  • Article 250
  • prevail over inconsistent State laws to the extent provided by Constitution.

60. Article 252

Parliament may legislate on a State List matter at the request of:

  • Two or more State Legislatures.

Other States may later:

  • Adopt that law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 252 → Two or More States Request Parliament

61. Article 253

Parliament may legislate on any subject, including State List matters, for implementing:

  • International treaties.
  • Agreements.
  • Conventions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 253 → International Obligations

62. President's Rule and State Legislation

During President's Rule under Article 356:

  • Parliament may exercise legislative authority for the concerned State according to constitutional procedure.

63. Article 255

The source describes Article 255 as dealing with procedural requirements concerning:

  • Recommendations.
  • Previous sanctions.
  • and notes that such requirements are generally treated as directory within the constitutional framework stated in the attachment.

64. Article 256

States must ensure compliance with:

  • Parliamentary laws.
  • Existing applicable laws.
  • Union may issue directions to States where constitutionally authorised.

65. Article 257

States must exercise executive power without:

  • Impeding Union executive power.
  • Union may issue directions in constitutionally authorised situations.

66. Article 258

The President may entrust:

  • Union functions

to:

  • State Governments
  • with their consent.

67. Article 258A

A State Governor, with consent of Government of India, may entrust:

  • State functions

to:

  • Union Government.

68. Article 261

Article 261 provides:

  • Full Faith and Credit

throughout India to:

  • Public Acts.
  • Records.
  • Judicial Proceedings.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 261 → Full Faith and Credit

69. Meaning of Cooperative Federalism

Cooperative Federalism means:

  • Union and States work together.
  • Policies are coordinated.
  • Common national objectives are pursued through consultation.

70. Objectives of Cooperative Federalism

It seeks to:

  • Strengthen national unity.
  • Improve policy coordination.
  • Promote balanced development.
  • Improve welfare implementation.
  • Resolve issues through consultation.

71. Features of Cooperative Federalism

Important features include:

  • Shared responsibilities.
  • Joint decision-making.
  • Mutual consultation.
  • Policy coordination.
  • Development partnership.
  • Respect for constitutional division of powers.

72. Examples of Cooperative Federalism

Examples mentioned in the attachment include:

  • GST Council.
  • NITI Aayog.
  • Inter-State Council.
  • Finance Commission.
  • Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
  • Disaster-management coordination.
  • National health programmes.

NITI Aayog was established in:

  • 2015.

It replaced:

  • Planning Commission.

It promotes:

  • Cooperative Federalism.
  • Shared policy formulation.
  • State participation.
  • Sustainable development.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → 2015 → Cooperative Federalism

74. NITI Aayog Governing Council

  • Governing Council.

Regional Councils may also facilitate:

  • Inter-governmental cooperation.

75. GST Council

Constitutional basis:

Members include:

  • Union Finance Minister.
  • Union Minister of State for Finance.
  • State Finance Ministers.

Article 279A → GST Council

76. GST Council Functions

The GST Council recommends matters such as:

  • GST rates.
  • Exemptions.
  • Tax administration.
  • Revenue-related arrangements.

77. GST Council and Federalism

The source identifies GST Council as an important example of:

  • Cooperative Federalism.
  • Fiscal cooperation.
  • Joint Union–State decision-making.

78. Competitive Federalism

Competitive Federalism means:

  • Healthy competition among States

to improve:

  • Governance.
  • Economic growth.
  • Investment.
  • Public services.
  • Innovation.

79. Objectives of Competitive Federalism

It encourages States to:

  • Improve administration.
  • Attract investment.
  • Generate employment.
  • Improve infrastructure.
  • Strengthen welfare.
  • Adopt best practices.

80. Areas of State Competition

Examples include:

  • Ease of Doing Business.
  • Startup ecosystem.
  • Industrial development.
  • Digital governance.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Tourism.
  • Investment promotion.

81. NITI Aayog and State Rankings

The source mentions indices such as:

  • SDG Index.
  • School Education Quality Index in earlier editions.
  • Health Index with relevant agencies.
  • Innovation Index.

These encourage:

  • Performance-based competition among States.

82. Benefits of Competitive Federalism

It can promote:

  • Better governance.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Innovation.
  • Investment.
  • Economic growth.
  • Better public-service delivery.

83. Challenges of Competitive Federalism

Excessive competition may cause:

  • Regional imbalance.
  • Unequal development.
  • Competition for scarce resources.
  • Fiscal stress.

Competition should therefore remain:

  • Healthy.
  • Constructive.

84. Fiscal Federalism

Fiscal Federalism refers to:

  • Constitutional distribution of financial powers and resources between Union and States.

85. Objectives of Fiscal Federalism

It seeks to:

  • Maintain financial balance.
  • Promote equitable development.
  • Reduce regional disparities.
  • Strengthen State finances.
  • Improve public services.

86. Finance Commission

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 280.

The Finance Commission is constituted by:

  • President.

Frequency:

  • Every five years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 280 → Finance Commission → President → Every 5 Years

87. Finance Commission Functions

The source identifies recommendations relating to:

  • Distribution of Central taxes.
  • Grants-in-aid.
  • Strengthening State finances.

88. Tax Devolution

Tax devolution means sharing of net proceeds of specified Central taxes between:

  • Union.
  • States.

The percentage is recommended by:

  • Finance Commission.

89. Grants-in-Aid

Grants may support:

  • Revenue deficit.
  • Disaster management.
  • Local governance.
  • Sector-specific needs.

90. GST and Fiscal Federalism

GST strengthened fiscal coordination by:

  • Creating a common indirect tax system.
  • Promoting joint decision-making.
  • Facilitating revenue sharing.
  • Reducing cascading of taxes.

91. GST Compensation

The source notes that:

  • States were provided compensation for specified transition-period revenue losses through relevant GST compensation legislation.
  • This was intended to maintain Union–State trust during GST implementation.

92. Cooperative vs Competitive Federalism

Cooperative Federalism:

  • Union and States work together.
  • Partnership.
  • Consultation.
  • Consensus.

Competitive Federalism:

  • States compete with one another.
  • Performance.
  • Innovation.
  • Reform.

93. Cooperative vs Fiscal Federalism

Cooperative Federalism:

  • Policy and administrative cooperation.

Fiscal Federalism:

  • Financial distribution between Union and States.

  • Article 279A.

101st Amendment → GST + 246A + 269A + 279A

The 101st Amendment strengthened:

  • Fiscal Federalism.
  • Joint decision-making.
  • Common national market.

139. State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963

The Supreme Court held:

  • India is not formed by an agreement among sovereign States.
  • States do not possess sovereignty independent of Constitution.
  • Parliament possesses constitutional authority within its assigned field.
📌 Must-Memorise

State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963 → Nature of Indian Union

140. Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon, 1972

The Supreme Court clarified:

  • Parliament possesses residuary legislative power over subjects not included in the three Lists.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 248.
  • Entry 97, Union List.
📌 Must-Memorise

H.S. Dhillon → 1972 → Residuary Powers

141. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973

The Supreme Court established:

  • Basic Structure Doctrine.
  • Parliament cannot destroy the Basic Structure through constitutional amendment.

142. Federalism as Basic Structure

The source states that:

  • Federalism forms part of the Basic Structure.
  • Parliament cannot abolish India's federal character through amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Federalism → Basic Structure

143. R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India, 1993

The Supreme Court recognised the permissibility of:

  • Asymmetrical Federalism.

Different constitutional arrangements may exist for:

  • Different States.
  • Different regions
  • based on historical and constitutional circumstances.
📌 Must-Memorise

R.C. Poudyal → 1993 → Asymmetrical Federalism

144. Meaning of Asymmetrical Federalism

Asymmetrical Federalism means:

  • Different States or regions may have different constitutional arrangements.
  • Uniformity is not always necessary for every unit of Federation.

145. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994

The Supreme Court held:

  • Federalism is part of Basic Structure.
  • Article 356 is subject to Judicial Review.
  • Majority should ordinarily be tested on floor of Legislative Assembly.
  • President's Rule cannot be used arbitrarily.
📌 Must-Memorise

146. Importance of S.R. Bommai

The judgment strengthened:

  • State autonomy.
  • Federalism.
  • Democratic government.
  • Judicial control over Union power.

147. Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, 2006

The Supreme Court held:

  • Domicile in a particular State is not mandatory for contesting Rajya Sabha election from that State.
  • Rajya Sabha is a federal chamber but differs from classical federal second chambers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kuldip Nayar → 2006 → Rajya Sabha Domicile Not Mandatory

The Supreme Court emphasised:

  • Cooperative Federalism.
  • Democratic accountability.
  • Lieutenant Governor should ordinarily act on aid and advice in matters within elected Government's legislative competence, subject to constitutional limitations.

149. Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India, 2023

The source records that the Supreme Court dealt with:

  • Distribution of executive authority in Delhi.

  • States are not independently sovereign.

  • Cooperative Federalism is constitutionally important.
  • State autonomy must coexist with national unity.
